questions.question: According to the ISPE Process Gases guide, which of the following best matches its scope?

options.A: Medical gases and breathing air for patient use, and steam used for sterilization, are the primary subjects of the guide and take priority
options.B: Gases in direct contact with biopharmaceutical and pharmaceutical process fluids, such as nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and compressed air
options.C: Only compressed air, and only for existing facilities that have been validated and comply with GMP
options.D: Gases used for all purposes in the plant, and used to replace the regulations, standards and codes that apply to such facilities in each country

questions.explanation: The guide covers nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and compressed air that are in direct contact with process fluids; medical gases, breathing air and steam are out of scope. The guide itself is neither a standard nor GMP, and does not replace regulations.

questions.question: To facilitate risk assessment, how does the guide view the output (gas) of a gas system for the purpose of applying CQAs and CPPs?

options.A: As a drug substance, so all gases must meet the pharmacopoeial monograph requirements for drug substances
options.B: As a packaging material, so only its appearance, supplier qualification and damage during delivery need to be assessed
options.C: As a pure utility, with no CQAs and CPPs applied and managed only through equipment specifications and vendor warranty
options.D: As an excipient, since the gas is in direct contact with the product or becomes part of the final formulation

questions.explanation: Section 1.5.1 explains that the guide treats the gas output of a system as an excipient because it is in direct contact with the product or becomes part of the formulation, which helps risk assessment.

questions.question: An engineer sees that commercially available dryers mostly achieve -40°C and writes -40°C directly as a CPP for process air. According to the guide, how is this practice regarded?

options.A: Not appropriate; the dewpoint requirement should be set according to process needs and not adopted merely because the equipment can achieve it
options.B: Appropriate, because -40°C is the uniform industry minimum requirement that all process air must meet
options.C: Appropriate, as long as the dryer supplier issues a certificate of conformity, which is sufficient basis for this CPP
options.D: Not appropriate, because dewpoint can only be listed as a business requirement and must never be listed as a CPP for any system

questions.explanation: Section 2.2 states that requirements should be based on product and process needs rather than on available equipment capability; -40°C should not be selected automatically as a CPP just because equipment can reach it. Moisture content and similar parameters may still be CPPs (example in 2.3).

questions.question: A URS states "Preferably use the company's usual PLC brand and model, with grey equipment color". Which category of requirement is this?

options.A: A quality requirement, because the control system brand directly determines the CQA of the gas
options.B: A business requirement, because it is a mandatory term like gas supply volume and pressure
options.C: A desired attribute, an optional requirement, which the project team can decide whether to keep in scope
options.D: A critical process parameter (CPP), because PLC settings affect gas purity at the point of use

questions.explanation: Section 2.3 divides URS items into quality requirements (CQA/CPP), business requirements and desired attributes; the usual PLC brand, instrument supplier and equipment color are optional desired attributes.

questions.question: What is the typical system requirement for user requirements on hydrocarbons in process gases?

options.A: ≤ 250 ppm, and never to be treated as a CQA, because the compressor already has an oil-water separator and no separate specification is needed
options.B: ≤ 25 ppm or non-detectable, with a lower value specified, or even treated as a CQA, if the process requires
options.C: ≤ 0.5 ppm, uniformly specified by the compressor supplier according to model, with no need for the user to assess it or include it in the URS
options.D: No specification is needed, because hydrocarbons in oxygen lines pose no risk to safety or quality and have no toxic effect

questions.explanation: Section 2.2 states that the typical requirement is ≤ 25 ppm or non-detectable, with the process deciding whether a lower value or a CQA is needed; hydrocarbons in oxygen lines carry an additional safety risk.

questions.question: What is the most common method of manufacturing nitrogen, oxygen and argon?

options.A: Obtained by water electrolysis and then purified by chemical reaction, in a facility called an air-separation unit, and delivered to users by tanker
options.B: Direct adsorption of air by molecular sieve at the user's site followed by freeze-drying purification, with no liquefaction step and no separation column
options.C: Liquefaction of air followed by fractional distillation, in a facility called an air-separation unit
options.D: Obtained directly from the atmosphere by membrane filtration and liquefied and stored at low temperature, with no separation column and no compressed air needed

questions.explanation: Section 3.2.2 states that nitrogen, oxygen and argon are most often made by fractional distillation of liquid air, in a facility commonly called an air-separation unit; electrolysis, molecular sieve and chemical reaction are only other possible methods.

questions.question: A cryogenic liquid storage tank is fitted with both a pressure relief valve and a rupture disk. What is the difference between them?

options.A: The relief valve closes automatically after relieving; the rupture disk bursts at a pressure higher than the relief valve setting and does not close again
options.B: The rupture disk operates at a pressure lower than the relief valve setting and resets automatically after operating to reduce gas loss, and can be reused
options.C: Both close automatically after relieving; the only difference is that the relief valve is on the inner tank and the rupture disk on the outer tank, with identical function
options.D: The relief valve must be replaced once it operates, while the rupture disk can be reused after pressure is restored, without replacing any parts

questions.explanation: Section 3.5.1.1: a spring-type relief valve closes automatically after relieving; a rupture disk bursts at a pressure above the relief valve setting as a backup, and once it operates it does not close again, so the entire contents of the tank may be released.

questions.question: What is the difference between the CoC (Certificate of Conformance) and the CoA (Certificate of Analysis) provided by a gas supplier?

options.A: Treated as a drug substance, so all gases must meet the pharmacopoeial monograph requirements for drug substances and be released batch by batch
options.B: Treated as a packaging material, so only appearance, supplier qualification and damage during delivery need to be assessed, with no need to assess purity
options.C: The CoC includes microbial and particulate test values for each batch; the CoA lists only the gas's purity and moisture content
options.D: The CoC states that the gas meets the minimum purity specification and usually contains no analytical results; the CoA gives the specification and the analytical results for that batch

questions.explanation: Section 3.6.1: a typical CoC only states that the gas meets the minimum purity specification and usually has no analytical results; a CoA gives the minimum specification and the specific analytical results for that batch.

questions.question: A nitrogen line leaks, and personnel on site should be alert to oxygen deficiency. According to the guide, below what oxygen concentration in air is an atmosphere defined as oxygen-deficient?

options.A: Below 23.5%
options.B: Below 19.5%
options.C: Below 21%
options.D: Below 15%

questions.explanation: Section 3.5.4: an oxygen concentration below 19.5% is oxygen-deficient; only above 23.5% is it oxygen-enriched. The main hazard of inert gases is displacement of oxygen in the air.

questions.topic: Microbial and particulate in source gas
questions.question: A supplier's gas specification certificate usually contains no microbial or particulate testing. If the user judges that these two are a concern for CQAs, how should this be handled according to the guide?

options.A: After a risk assessment determines it is a critical-to-quality concern, take appropriate system design and operating measures
options.B: Require the gas supplier to measure each batch at the manufacturing site and list microbial and particulate results on the certificate as a release condition
options.C: Because the supplier regards it as low risk, the user need not do any further assessment or take any system design or operating measures
options.D: Always install a 0.2 µm sterilizing-grade filter at the tank outlet, and use that in place of the original risk assessment

questions.explanation: Section 3.6.1: microorganisms and particulates are usually not measured in source gas specifications and suppliers regard them as low risk; but if the user determines through risk assessment that they are critical-to-quality, appropriate system design and operating measures should be taken.

questions.question: When a lubricant-injected screw compressor is used to supply process air, what is the oil content of the discharge and the corresponding measure?

options.A: The discharge contains no oil, since the lubricant is used only for cooling and sealing, so no filtration or oil-water separation is needed downstream
options.B: The discharge contains about 25-50 ppm of oil, and an oil-free compressor must be used instead; it cannot be handled by filtration or remedied by maintenance
options.C: The discharge contains about 2-5 ppm of oil, which can be removed simply by raising the aftercooler outlet temperature, without filtration
options.D: The discharge usually contains 2-5 ppm of entrained lubricant, so coalescing filters should be used

questions.explanation: Section 4.3.4: the discharge of a lubricant-injected compressor usually contains 2-5 ppm of entrained lubricant, so coalescing filters should be used; maintenance of oil-water separation and condensate drainage must also be considered.

questions.question: In a twin-tower regenerative-desiccant dryer, what are the approximate purge air amounts for the heatless, heated and blower purge types, respectively?

options.D: All three types about 15%, differing only in initial cost

questions.explanation: Section 4.6.1: heatless needs about 15% of capacity as purge; heated reduces this to 7 or 8%; blower purge can reduce it to 0-2%, but the cost may be successively higher.

questions.question: A plant plans to use a single-vessel heat-of-compression dryer to supply process air. The URS requires a -40°C dewpoint, but demand load varies. How should this be handled according to the guide?

options.A: It can be used directly, since its built-in twin-tower switching maintains a constant -40°C dewpoint regardless of load
options.B: The dewpoint also varies with load, so a risk assessment should compare the maximum allowable dewpoint with the highest dewpoint this type may reach at different loads
options.C: A refrigerant dryer should be used instead, since its dewpoint range of about 3-10°C can steadily meet the -40°C requirement
options.D: Increasing the capacity of the downstream air receiver guarantees that the dewpoint stays at -40°C under any load

questions.explanation: Section 4.6.2.1: the single-vessel type has no tower switching, so the dewpoint also varies as load varies and it is unlikely to provide a constant -40°C; a risk assessment should compare the maximum allowable dewpoint with the highest dewpoint it may reach.

questions.question: Why are refrigerant dryers seldom used for pharmaceutical process air?

options.A: Because their dewpoint is about 3°C to 10°C, whereas process air usually needs a much lower dewpoint
options.B: Because both their initial cost and operating cost are significantly higher than those of desiccant dryers, so they are uneconomical
options.C: Because they must regenerate the desiccant with hot compressed air, losing a large amount of compressed air and so being uneconomical
options.D: Because although their dewpoint can reach -40°C, they cannot run continuously and must be shut down periodically for regeneration

questions.explanation: Section 4.6.3: refrigerant dryers have low initial and operating costs, but their dewpoint is only 3-10°C, and process air usually needs a much lower dewpoint, so they are seldom used.

questions.question: What is the rule of thumb for the capacity of an air receiver?

options.A: About 1-2 times the compressor peak capacity (free air delivered/second)
options.B: About 60-90 times the compressor peak capacity (free air delivered/second)
options.C: The same as the compressor peak capacity (free air delivered/second), plus twice the dryer purge air consumption
options.D: About 6-10 times the compressor peak capacity (free air delivered/second)

questions.explanation: Section 4.8: the rule of thumb is to select a receiver with a capacity of 6 to 10 times the compressor peak capacity (free air delivered/second). The 60-90 seconds refers to the duration of a brief demand peak, not a multiplier.

questions.question: Compared with a one-way distribution, why is a ring main considered a more robust distribution design?

options.A: It has two supply sources, the system can self-balance, and well-placed isolation valves allow maintenance without shutting down the whole loop
options.B: It has only a single supply source, but the pipe diameter can be greatly reduced, so construction cost is always lower than a one-way design
options.C: The loop itself has no buffer capacity, so an additional intermediate receiver must be added to cope with high demand
options.D: It cannot connect multiple compressors, so its redundancy is lower than a one-way design, though it is easy to maintain

questions.explanation: Section 5.1.2.2: a ring main has two supply sources, can self-balance and optimize pipe size; well-placed isolation valves allow local maintenance; the loop itself has buffer capacity and can also connect multiple gas sources for added redundancy.

questions.question: Which statement on the calculation of distribution pipe size and typical values is correct according to the guide?

options.A: Based on maximum usage, typical values are about 0.6-0.9 m/s or 30-50 psi pressure drop, independent of filter pressure drop, which need not be considered
options.B: It can be calculated from maximum velocity or allowable pressure drop, with typical values of about 6-9 m/s or 3-5 psi, and the increased pressure drop of fouled filters must be considered
options.C: Based only on the number of POUs, with typical values of about 20 m/s or more to reduce pipe size, pressure drop need not be considered, and filters need not be a concern
options.D: Based only on pipe length, with typical values of about 1-2 m/s, and the greater the pressure drop the lower the compressor energy consumption and operating cost

questions.explanation: Section 5.1.2.5: pipe size can be calculated from maximum velocity or allowable pressure drop, typically 6-9 m/s or 3-5 psi; the greater the pressure drop, the higher the required supply pressure and energy consumption, and pressure drop when filters are fouled must also be considered.

questions.question: When sterile gas or sterile vent is required, what type of filter is usually placed, and where?

options.A: A 0.2 µm hydrophilic filter at the gas source, with no further filter needed at the point of use, no integrity test, and no additional verification
options.B: Only a 1 µm filter at the compressor inlet, after which the distribution piping can be considered sterile, with no separate point-of-use filter
options.C: A 0.2 µm hydrophobic sterilizing-grade filter at the point of delivery/use
options.D: A 5 µm coarse filter at the point of use, with the whole distribution line sterilized by SIP in place of sterilizing-grade filtration

questions.explanation: Section 5.5.1: the distribution system is usually protected by a 1 µm or finer filter at the source; when sterile gas or vent is required, this is usually achieved with a 0.2 µm hydrophobic sterilizing-grade filter at the point of use.

questions.question: Which test is most suitable for testing a sterilized hydrophobic gas filter in situ, without using alcohol and without contaminating the downstream side?

options.A: A Bubble Point test, wetting the membrane with 70% IPA/30% water solution and then increasing pressure gradually
options.B: A Forward Flow (Diffusion) test, measuring gas flow slightly below the Bubble Point on a wetted membrane
options.C: A destructive test with bacterial aerosol challenge, with the filter replaced after the test
options.D: A Water Intrusion Test, measuring the flow of water through a dry hydrophobic membrane using water and air overpressure

questions.explanation: Section 5.5.2.3: the Water Intrusion Test uses no low-surface-tension liquid such as alcohol and does not contaminate the downstream side of an intact filter, making it especially suitable for in situ testing of sterile hydrophobic membranes; Bubble Point and Forward Flow require wetting the membrane.

questions.question: A system has an inlet pressure of 14 bar (about 200 psi) that must be reduced to 3.5 bar, and the inlet pressure fluctuates widely. What pressure reduction approach does the guide recommend?

options.A: Use a single pressure reducing valve, since valve life is unrelated to the size of the pressure difference and pressure regulation accuracy is unaffected, with no need for series arrangement or to consider inlet pressure fluctuation
options.B: Use two pressure reducing valves in parallel so each valve bears half of the pressure difference and output pressure is also more stable, at no additional cost
options.C: Use two pressure reducing valves in series (two-stage serial reduction), so that no single valve bears the extreme pressure difference
options.D: Use a mixing valve to blend high-pressure and low-pressure gas to reduce pressure and maintain gas purity, with no other valves and no need to consider the pressure difference

questions.explanation: Section 5.3.1: when the inlet pressure is ≥ 200 psi (14 bar), the reduction ratio exceeds 4:1, or the inlet pressure fluctuates greatly, two-stage serial reduction is recommended, giving longer valve life and more accurate pressure regulation.

questions.question: Why does the guide consider pressure generally an engineering parameter rather than a CPP?

options.A: Because pressure does not affect any downstream equipment, so the system needs no pressure monitoring at all, no alarms, and no additional verification
options.B: Because equipment with specific flow or pressure requirements has its own inlet pressure switch and alarm, so system pressure control provides only general indication
options.C: Because pressure can be measured only at the compressor outlet, cannot be calibrated and cannot be included in any monitoring program, so it is unimportant
options.D: Because regulations explicitly prohibit listing pressure as a CPP, and all process gas systems must comply without exception

questions.explanation: Section 6.3.1: equipment that needs a specific flow/pressure has its own inlet pressure switch and alarm (a critical location/instrument); system pressure control does not monitor each POU, so pressure is usually an engineering parameter.

questions.question: A process gas system operates at a very low dewpoint. According to the concept of water activity (aw), which statement is correct?

options.A: Bacteria do not grow below aw 0.6, and molds and yeasts do not grow below aw 0.85
options.B: Low aw kills all microorganisms, including bacteria that can form endospores, so no microbial monitoring is needed
options.C: Low aw makes microorganisms grow faster but cannot keep them alive, so only the presence of condensate in the system needs monitoring
options.D: Bacteria do not grow below aw 0.85, and molds and yeasts do not grow below aw 0.6

questions.explanation: Section 6.3.2: molds and yeasts do not grow at aw < 0.6 and bacteria do not grow at aw < 0.85; however, dryness only inhibits, and microorganisms (such as endospores) may still survive, so it cannot be regarded as sterilization.

questions.question: When nitrogen is used for blanketing in sterile filling, how should the process gas sampling point be planned according to the guide?

options.A: Upstream of the final sterilizing filter, because gas quality is the same before and after the filter, and sampling downstream of the filter carries risk every time
options.B: Downstream of the final sterilizing filter, sharing a line with pure steam so the sample point can be sterilized with the line
options.C: Downstream of the final sterilizing filter, sharing a line with highly purified water to reduce the number of sampling points needed on site
options.D: No risk assessment is needed for the location; being close to the compressor and convenient for sampling is enough to represent point-of-use quality, with no need to demonstrate it

questions.explanation: Section 6.3.2.1: nitrogen sampling for aseptic operations should be upstream of the final sterilizing filter; sampling downstream of the filter needs the same level of sterility as the unit operation, and every sampling carries risk. Sampling points should also avoid sharing lines with highly purified water or pure steam.

questions.question: Which statement on the microbial monitoring focus for different gases is correct according to the guide?

options.A: N2, CO2 and Ar need only be monitored for aerobic microorganisms; process air and O2 need monitoring for microorganisms that can grow anaerobically, and only during the performance testing phase
options.B: All gases need only be monitored for aerobic microorganisms, regardless of gas type, oxygen content or process risk
options.C: Low-oxygen gases such as N2, CO2 and Ar should be monitored for microorganisms that can grow anaerobically; process air and O2 for aerobic microorganisms
options.D: N2, CO2 and Ar have low oxygen content and do not support any microorganisms, so no microbial monitoring or sampling is needed at all

questions.explanation: Section 6.3.2.1: process air and O2 should be monitored for aerobic microorganisms; low-oxygen gases such as N2, CO2 and Ar should be monitored for those able to grow anaerobically. Aerobic microorganisms should also be considered during performance testing.

questions.question: When nitrogen is used for safety purposes (such as inerting), what is the maximum oxygen content the guide considers acceptable?

options.A: Up to 5%
options.B: Up to 0.1%
options.C: Up to 10%
options.D: Up to 1%

questions.explanation: Section 6.3.2.7: when nitrogen is used for safety purposes, oxygen up to 1% is considered acceptable; when used as a product blanketing gas it should meet pharmacopoeial purity requirements.

questions.question: During performance testing, how many times should each point of use (POU) be sampled at a minimum?

options.A: Once; the test passes if the result meets the acceptance criteria, with no need to repeat sampling
options.B: Twice consecutively, each time witnessed on site by quality unit personnel to be valid
options.C: At least three consecutive times over a defined period, evaluated against pre-defined acceptance criteria
options.D: Ten consecutive times, after passing which any subsequent reduction in monitoring frequency is allowed and before which no adjustment is permitted

questions.explanation: Section 8.5: performance testing is usually sampling of each POU under normal operating conditions, with each POU sampled at least three consecutive times over a defined period, and the data evaluated against pre-defined acceptance criteria.

questions.question: According to the guide, who usually approves commissioning documents in advance?

options.A: Relevant SMEs of the organization's engineering team; for large projects the project manager may be added, and quality unit pre-approval is usually not needed
options.B: Always the quality unit, without whose pre-approval commissioning activities may not begin
options.C: Only the external contractor, because the organization's own staff may not take part in commissioning activities
options.D: Approval from the regulatory authority must first be obtained, otherwise the system may not proceed to performance testing even when complete

questions.explanation: Section 8.3: commissioning documents may be pre-approved by engineering SMEs, with the project manager added for large projects (for contractual reasons); quality unit pre-approval is usually not needed.

questions.question: When testing a process gas system, how does the guide view its comparison with water or steam systems?

options.A: They are similar, so the requirements for water systems should be followed and dead legs, slope and surface roughness tested one by one against the same standards
options.B: They are fundamentally different and comparison should be avoided; drainability, dead legs or surface roughness usually need not be tested
options.C: They are identical, with liquid simply replaced by gas, so all test items and acceptance criteria must be the same and no item may be omitted
options.D: Only surface roughness needs to be tested as for water systems, and all other items can be omitted because of gas flow, though slope and dead legs must still be verified

questions.explanation: Section 8.1: process gas systems are fundamentally different from water and steam systems, and comparison should be avoided; from a quality standpoint, drainability/sloping, dead legs, MoC or surface roughness usually need not be tested.

questions.question: In the risk assessment process, what does risk analysis mean?

options.A: Comparing the analyzed risk with pre-given risk criteria to judge its significance, expressed as high, medium or low
options.B: Identifying potential hazards and describing their possible consequences, answering "what might go wrong", and assigning responsible persons
options.C: Deciding whether to reduce or accept the risk and implementing controls to bring the risk to an acceptable level, while notifying the regulatory authority
options.D: Estimating risk, qualitatively or quantitatively, by linking the severity, likelihood of occurrence and detectability of a hazard

questions.explanation: Section 7.3.3: risk analysis is the estimation of risk for identified hazards, linking severity, likelihood of occurrence and the ability to detect the hazard, qualitatively or quantitatively; comparison with criteria is risk evaluation (Section 7.3.4).

questions.question: Regarding the use of differential pressure in a maintenance plan to decide when to change general filters, which statement is correct according to the guide?

options.A: Using differential pressure alone as the only indicator is not necessarily good practice, unless it is monitored at a known gas flow
options.B: Differential pressure is the only acceptable change indicator and applies regardless of the gas flow at the time, with no additional verification needed
options.C: Filters need not be changed periodically; they need attention only when the differential pressure alarm sounds
options.D: Only POU filters need changing; general filters can be used until the system is retired, with no change frequency

questions.explanation: Section 9.1.1.2: filters should be changed periodically, with the frequency depending on usage; using differential pressure as the only change indicator is not necessarily appropriate, unless it is monitored at a known gas flow.

questions.question: A system operates at a -40°C pressure dewpoint, 6 bar and ambient 21°C. What are the approximate relative humidity and aw of the air?

options.A: About 50% RH, aw about 0.5
options.B: About 0.5% RH, aw about 0.005
options.C: About 85% RH, aw about 0.85
options.D: About 5% RH, aw about 0.05

questions.explanation: Appendix 1 Section 10.6: at -40°C DP, about 6 bar and ambient 21°C, the air is about 5% RH, i.e. aw 0.05, so neither bacteria nor molds can multiply.

questions.question: In the Appendix 1 example, how is the pressure test of the compressed air distribution pipework carried out?

options.A: At about 0.5 times the maximum operating pressure, only once during construction and not repeated afterwards, with no separate risk assessment
options.B: At about 1.5 times the normal maximum operating pressure, with leak testing repeated afterwards during periodic maintenance of the system
options.C: At about 3 times the maximum operating pressure, not repeated afterwards because the pipework is metallic
options.D: At the same pressure as the operating pressure, repeated before each use

questions.explanation: Appendix 1 Section 10.3: during construction all pipework is pressure tested at about 1.5 times the normal maximum operating pressure, and leak testing is repeated during periodic maintenance to confirm system integrity.

questions.question: In the Appendix 1 example, to confirm there is no moisture ingress into the distribution pipework, where should moisture content be measured in addition to sampling after the dryer?

options.A: Only at the compressor inlet, since moisture can only come from outside air
options.B: At the outlet closest to the dryer, since the shortest pipework gives the results that are easiest to interpret, with no additional verification needed
options.C: At the outlet farthest from the dryer with the longest pipework, since it has the largest surface area and the greatest chance of moisture ingress
options.D: Continuously at every outlet throughout the year, since metallic pipework cannot block outside moisture

questions.explanation: Appendix 1 Section 10.3: metallic pipework is a very robust moisture barrier; integrity is confirmed by moisture content after the dryer and at the outlet with the longest pipework. This performance does not change with use of the pipework, so routine monitoring is not needed, but the PDP monitor is a critical instrument.

questions.question: In the Appendix 3 calibration example, how is the low pressure switch at the air purifier outlet classified and managed?

options.A: Treated as safety critical, calibrated annually, with its alarm functionally verified
options.B: Treated as non-critical, for engineering information only, so no calibration is needed
options.C: Treated as product critical, calibrated quarterly and verified with a standard gas source before each use
options.D: Treated as information only, with visual inspection only and replacement when damaged

questions.explanation: Appendix 3 Section 12: the low pressure switch triggers an alarm and is regarded as safety critical, so it will be calibrated annually with its alarm functionally verified; information-only flow meters and pressure gauges need no routine calibration.

questions.question: How does the Appendix 2 risk assessment example treat system pressure?

options.A: Pressure is the main CPP of the system, and monitoring instruments must be installed at every outlet
options.B: Pressure is not regarded as a critical parameter of the system; if a downstream system needs it, that system has its own pressure monitoring device
options.C: Pressure is continuously monitored at each POU by the system controller and included in quality change control, with no separate risk assessment needed
options.D: Pressure is measured only at the dryer outlet and listed as one of the most important CQAs

questions.explanation: Appendix 2 Section 11: pressure is not considered a critical parameter for the system; if it is critical to the function of a downstream system, that system will have its own pressure monitoring, because monitoring every outlet is not practical.

questions.question: In the Appendix 4 URS template, in which section should the system boundaries be written?

options.A: 2.0 Purpose and Scope, briefly describing the project scope and system boundaries
options.B: 1.0 Introduction and Background, explaining the origin of the project and time requirements
options.C: 5.0 Process Description, a high-level description of the process using the gas
options.D: 4.0 Responsibilities, describing specific responsibilities other than the approvers

questions.explanation: Section 2.0 Purpose and Scope of the URS template briefly describes the project scope and related product requirements and describes the system boundaries (what is included in scope); 1.0 covers the project background and schedule, and 5.0 the process description.

questions.question: What does Appendix 5 recommend about leaks in process gas systems?

options.A: Leaks can be eliminated completely, and a single pressure test after construction guarantees that no leak will occur later
options.B: Losses from small leaks are negligible, so no ongoing leak detection program or pressure test is needed
options.C: Leaks are very hard to eliminate completely; design aims to reduce leakage, and a post-construction pressure test and an ongoing leak detection program reduce losses
options.D: Leaks cannot be reduced and can only be compensated for by increasing compressor capacity, so no special handling or detection is needed at the design stage

questions.explanation: Appendix 5 Section 14.1: it is difficult to eliminate leaks entirely, so the design goal is to reduce them; a post-construction pressure test and an ongoing leak detection program can reduce losses, which for pressurized gas can be considerable.

questions.question: Of the three nitrogen generation principles introduced in Appendix 6, what is the nitrogen purity range that the membrane process can produce?

options.A: 98% to 99.99% or higher
options.B: 1 to 100 ppm oxygen
options.C: Above 99.999%, with no oxygen content limit

questions.explanation: Appendix 6 Section 15: membrane purity is about 95% to 99.5%; adsorption is about 98% to 99.99% or higher; cryogenic is about 1 to 100 ppm oxygen.

questions.question: According to the glossary, what is blanketing?

options.A: Continuously passing gas through the product liquid to remove dissolved oxygen and reduce water content, together with a sterilization treatment
options.B: Placing a layer of gas (usually nitrogen) in the headspace above the product in a vessel, often used to keep oxygen in the air from contacting and degrading the product
options.C: Covering the outside of piping with insulation to avoid condensation inside and outside the pipe for low-dewpoint gas, thereby reducing compressor energy consumption
options.D: Pressurizing gas into a vessel above atmospheric pressure for leak and integrity testing of the system and to confirm pressure is held

questions.explanation: Appendix 9 Section 18.2: blanketing is placing a layer of gas (usually nitrogen) in the space above the product in a vessel, generally to keep oxygen in the air from contacting and degrading the product, and it can also maintain a low-oxygen atmosphere to reduce explosion risk.

questions.question: According to the glossary, what is the definition of dewpoint?

options.A: The temperature to which water must be heated to vaporize completely, so it is a fixed value independent of pressure and unaffected by humidity
options.B: The temperature of the compressor discharge at the aftercooler outlet, used to express how dry the air is
options.C: The temperature to which moist air must be cooled, at constant atmospheric pressure, for its water vapor to condense into water; a saturation temperature
options.D: The temperature at which moisture in the air freezes, independent of air pressure and meaningful only below 0°C

questions.explanation: Appendix 9 Section 18.2: dewpoint is the temperature to which a parcel of moist air must be cooled, at constant atmospheric pressure, for its water vapor to condense into water (the condensed water being dew); it is a saturation temperature.
